Pepsin. A serine protease secreted in the stomach that catalyzes the hydrolysis of peptide bonds in proteins, initiating protein digestion. It functions in the highly acidic stomach environment with a pH between one-point-five and two-point-five, and is notably specific for hydrophobic residues flanking the peptide bond. Pepsin catalyzes hydrolysis of peptide bonds, especially those adjacent to aromatic or branched-chain amino acids like phenylalanine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and leucine. Its substrate is proteins and polypeptides, beginning digestion before other proteases take over in the small intestine. The enzyme is produced as an inactive zymogen called pepsinogen in stomach chief cells. Low pH and a process called autocleavage activate pepsinogen into pepsin. Pepsin's pH optimum is one-point-five to two-point-five. The native enzyme denatures and irreversibly inactivates at neutral pH. The products of pepsin digestion are large peptide fragments, typically ten to thirty or more amino acids. Pepsin does not achieve complete amino acid liberation—that task is accomplished later by pancreatic proteases. The mechanism involves an aspartic protease active site containing two catalytic aspartate residues that facilitate nucleophilic attack on the peptide carbonyl. Peptic ulcers result from pepsin-induced tissue damage when the stomach's protective mechanisms are compromised. Pepsin represents an elegant adaptation to gastric digestion. It functions optimally in an environment where most proteins are denatured and most enzymes are destroyed. The stomach's extreme acidity itself serves protective functions—killing pathogens and providing an antiseptic barrier. Pepsin's specificity for hydrophobic positions reflects the prevalence of hydrophobic residues in protein interiors. By preferentially cleaving bonds that expose these residues, pepsin opens up the protein structure, accelerating subsequent digestion by intestinal proteases.
